facts.text: On this date in 1918, Latvia declared independence from Russia — it would be absorbed by the Soviet Union just 22 years later, then reclaim that independence in 1991 after 51 years of occupation.
On this date in 1477, William Caxton printed the first book in England. Within 50 years, over 20 million books circulated a continent that had fewer than 100 million people.
Manila is the world's most densely populated city proper, packing roughly 71,000 people per square kilometer — denser than any neighborhood in New York or Tokyo.
More people live inside a 4,000km circle centered on Bangladesh than live outside it. Over half of humanity fits within that single ring.
Canada has more lakes than every other country on Earth combined, holding about 60% of the world's fresh surface water — yet ranks among the highest per-capita water consumers.
On this day in 1928, Mickey Mouse debuted in 'Steamboat Willie' — the IP now anchors a Disney empire worth over $150B, all from an eight-minute cartoon.
On this day in 1963, the first push-button telephone went on sale. AT&T charged extra for the upgrade, turning a convenience into a revenue line.
The S&P 500 has historically risen more often than not on any given day — roughly 53% of trading days close green, yet most investors remember only the red ones.
Berkshire Hathaway's Class A share once traded for under $8. It now trades above $700,000 — Buffett has never split it, deliberately filtering out short-term traders.
The Dutch East India Company paid an 18% dividend in its first year, 1602. It remained the world's most valuable company for over a century, adjusted for nothing.
On this date in 1883, the US and Canada adopted standardized time zones — before that, every city set its own clocks by the sun, making rail schedules a chaos of hundreds of local times.
On this date in 1307, William Tell supposedly shot the apple. The crossbow bolt would have traveled at roughly 150 mph — enough to cleave a 1-inch target at 80 paces with period-accurate equipment.
A neutron star packs more mass than the Sun into a sphere the size of a city. A teaspoon of its material would weigh about a billion tons on Earth.
Your body replaces roughly 3.8 million red blood cells every second. Each one lives about 120 days, circling your body roughly 170,000 times before being dismantled by your spleen.
Light leaving the Sun takes 8 minutes to reach Earth but spent roughly 100,000 years traveling from the Sun's core to its surface first.
On this day in 1978, 918 people died at Jonestown — more American civilians lost in a single day than any event between WWII and 9/11.
Oxford University was already 300 years old when the Aztec Empire was founded.
On this day in 1883, the US adopted standardized time zones. Before that, every city ran its own clock.
Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the construction of the Great Pyramid.
The fax machine was invented in 1843 — 26 years before the transcontinental railroad was completed.
Saudade (Portuguese): a melancholic longing for something beloved that may never return. Untranslatable into English, it became the emotional spine of an entire musical genre — fado.
Hiraeth (Welsh): homesickness for a home you cannot return to, or perhaps never had. The word folds grief, longing, and belonging into a single breath no English word can match.
On this day in 1477, William Caxton printed the first dated book in English — introducing 'imprint' to the language, the word for a publisher's mark, from Latin imprimere, to press into.
Vellichor: coined by John Koenig in The Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows, it describes the strange wistfulness of a used bookshop. Invented words that feel ancient are called neologisms with patina.
Apricity: the warmth of winter sun on your skin. Recorded in Henry Cockeram's 1623 English dictionary, it quietly vanished from use — a perfect word the language simply forgot to keep.

On this date in 2017, Bitcoin's mempool backlog peaked above 200,000 unconfirmed transactions as the bull run overwhelmed block capacity — directly accelerating the SegWit adoption that had stalled for months.
On this date in 2021, El Salvador's Bitcoin bonds ('Volcano Bonds') were formally announced by President Bukele, denominated at $1B with a 6.5% coupon and a planned bitcoin yield layer on top.

Ethereum's EIP-1559, deployed in August 2021, destroyed over 4.4 million ETH in base fees by 2026 — making Ethereum net deflationary during periods of high network activity without any supply cap in its code.

Satoshi Nakamoto's original Bitcoin whitepaper never uses the word 'blockchain' — the data structure is called a 'chain of blocks', and the single-word compound entered common usage through third-party commentary.

The DAO hack in June 2016 drained 3.6 million ETH through a reentrancy bug — but the attacker was bound by the same 28-day withdrawal delay they exploited, giving the Ethereum community time to fork before funds moved.

On this date in 2022, OpenAI released ChatGPT. It reached 1 million users in 5 days — faster than any consumer product in history — and rewrote the product roadmap of nearly every major tech company within 90 days.
On this date in 1994, checkers was solved by Chinook, the first program to provably master a classic game. It took 18 years of computation and an endgame database of 39 trillion positions.
GPT-4 was trained on roughly 25,000 A100 GPUs for an estimated 90–100 days. The electricity alone cost more than most countries spend on scientific research annually.

AlphaFold 2 predicted the structures of over 200 million proteins — essentially the entire known proteome — in roughly 18 months. Experimental methods would have taken thousands of years at previous throughput.
The word 'perceptron' appeared in a 1958 New York Times headline predicting machines that walk, talk, and are conscious. The hype cycle predates the internet by four decades.
